claims.text: The MTP-FEP approach is applicable across the high-entropy-alloy family.
The initial TaVCrW alloy is a disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy.
An MTP for the liquid phase can achieve training errors below 1 meV/atom.
The MTP closely reproduces the ab initio phase-space distribution of multicomponent liquid alloys.
The MTP captures the relevant atomic interactions more accurately than EAM.
Low variance between MTP and DFT energies allows FEP free-energy calculations to converge rapidly.
The MTP-FEP approach can accurately calculate melting temperatures.
The MTP-FEP approach can accurately calculate enthalpies of fusion.
The MTP-FEP approach can accurately calculate entropies of fusion.
The MTP-FEP approach can accurately calculate volume changes at melting.
The MTP-FEP approach can accurately calculate liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
The approach will reduce computational-resource use by approximately 80% relative to TOR-TILD.
The approach will provide approximately a 20-fold speedup relative to TOR-TILD.
MTP-FEP and EAM-TI free-energy differences will be within 0.5 meV/atom.
A density-of-states gap at the Fermi level produces a critical electronic Gibbs-energy contribution.
Electronic excitations cause a melting-temperature shift of 48–57 K.
Solid-state short-range order stabilizes the alloy by approximately 2.4 meV/atom.
Solid-state short-range order contributes only about 25 K to the melting-point shift.
High-temperature magnetic fluctuations have negligible thermodynamic impact.
GGA/LDA treatment of elements such as V and Cr introduces deviations relative to CALPHAD data.

contradictions.description: An 80% resource saving is not equivalent to the stated approximately 20-fold speedup: under comparable resource-rate assumptions, a 20-fold speedup corresponds to about a 95% reduction in computational resources, whereas an 80% reduction corresponds to about a 5-fold speedup.
